subsection: 4. Economic and social challenges of the 1970s and 1980s: Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald

notes.b: The decade opened with EEC entry and ended with a second oil crisis, which made the economy hard to manage.
points: The oil crisis of 1973 followed the Arab-Israeli war of October 1973, when oil-producing states restricted supply and raised prices sharply.
A second oil crisis in 1979 followed the Iranian Revolution, pushing up fuel and energy costs again.
Inflation rose through the decade, and unemployment grew, especially after 1973, as industries that depended on cheap energy and export markets struggled.
Public spending rose faster than tax revenue, so the state borrowed heavily to fund services and welfare.
The national debt grew in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and interest payments on it became a large part of government spending.

notes.b: Lynch succeeded Seán Lemass as Taoiseach and led Fianna Fáil to victory in 1977.
points: John Mary Lynch was Taoiseach from November 1966 to March 1973, and again from December 1977 to December 1979.
He led Fianna Fáil to a large majority in the 1977 general election, after the government of Liam Cosgrave lost office.

The Arms Crisis of May 1970 began when Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney from the cabinet over alleged plans to import arms for Northern nationalists; Haughey was later tried and acquitted, and Captain James Kelly and Albert Luykx were the other people charged.
Lynch took a moderate line on Northern Ireland, rejecting the use of force by the state and seeking a political settlement; he was criticised by hardliners within Fianna Fáil.
After Bloody Sunday on 30 January 1972, a crowd burned the British embassy in Dublin, and Lynch condemned the violence while the British government called for restraint.
Contemporaries saw him as a calm and cautious leader; historians judge him as a skilled party manager whose government was weakened by the Arms Crisis and the economic shocks of the 1970s.

notes.b: Haughey was the dominant figure in Fianna Fáil during the 1980s and led the party through three governments.
points: Haughey was Minister for Finance under Lynch from 1966 to 1970, and he was later dismissed in the Arms Crisis.
He became Taoiseach in December 1979, after Lynch's resignation, and led a minority Fianna Fáil government until June 1981.
A 1980 speech by Haughey warned that Ireland was living beyond its means, and he proposed cuts in public spending to reduce borrowing.
His government of 1982 was short-lived, and the GUBU label, coined by Conor Cruise O'Brien, described the controversies of 1982 (see the notes on the political instability of 1981–1982).
Haughey returned as Taoiseach in March 1987 at the head of a minority government, and it agreed the Programme for National Recovery with unions and employers later that year.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters saw him as a shrewd politician and nationalist, while critics saw him as a spendthrift who had weakened public finances.
Historians tend to judge his economic record harshly, though the 1987 agreement is seen as the start of the recovery that followed in the 1990s.

notes.b: FitzGerald led the Fine Gael and Labour coalitions of 1981–82 and 1982–87, and he is remembered for his constitutional and northern initiatives.
points: FitzGerald was Taoiseach from June 1981 to March 1982, then again from December 1982 to March 1987.
He led the first coalition with Labour and then a second coalition with Labour, which lasted until the 1987 general election.
His government pursued a policy of reducing public spending and borrowing, though it struggled to stop rising unemployment.
He launched a constitutional crusade in the early 1980s, promoting a new Ireland based on pluralism and a secular approach to some constitutional issues.
The New Ireland Forum (1983–1984) brought together the main nationalist parties in the Republic and the SDLP in Northern Ireland to produce a report on the future of the island.

The Anglo-Irish Agreement was signed by FitzGerald and Margaret Thatcher on 15 November 1985, giving the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland affairs (see the notes on Anglo-Irish relations).

Contemporaries praised his intellectual approach, but unionists and some nationalists opposed the agreement; historians see him as a reforming Taoiseach whose economic record was less successful than his political agenda.
There were three general elections in less than two years: June 1981, February 1982 and November 1982.
The 1982 minority governments depended on the support of independent TDs to stay in office.
The period saw a series of political crises that brought down governments in 1981 and 1982.
The instability reflected the economic crisis, the rise in unemployment and emigration, and the lack of clear support for any one party.
The 1983 referendum inserted the Eighth Amendment into the Constitution, recognising the right to life of the unborn; it was passed by a clear majority on 7 September 1983.
The 1986 divorce referendum was defeated in June 1986, when voters rejected a proposal to allow divorce, which had been put forward by the government.
Both referendums were shaped by the Catholic Church's influence on Irish politics and by growing debate over secularisation and pluralism.
Unemployment reached high levels in the mid-1980s, with the rate passing about 15 per cent by the middle of the decade (about, verify).
Emigration returned on a large scale in the 1980s, with young people leaving for Britain, the United States and Australia.
The government's spending cuts and tax increases reduced the state's borrowing but also reduced employment in the public sector.
Ireland's public debt rose to a high share of national income by the mid-1980s, and interest payments on it became a major government cost.

notes.h: Assessment: the leadership of the 1970s and 1980s
points: Lynch's achievements: keeping the state stable through the Troubles and the Arms Crisis, and taking Ireland into the EEC in 1973.
Haughey's achievements: the 1987 Programme for National Recovery, and his role in making the party's nationalism a central part of its appeal.
FitzGerald's achievements: the New Ireland Forum, the Anglo-Irish Agreement and his push for a more open, pluralist state.
Limits: the economic crises of the 1970s and 1980s were not solved by any of the three leaders, and each left the public finances in difficulty.
Contemporary view: voters punished governments that cut spending or raised taxes, and they rewarded promises of new services in some elections.
Later view: historians judge the 1980s as a decade of lost growth, though they often credit the late 1980s agreements with laying foundations for recovery.
